text: The Haunted Mansion is a horror-themed dark-ride attraction located at Disneyland, Magic Kingdom, and Tokyo Disneyland. The ride features a ride-through tour in Omnimover vehicles known as "Doom Buggies" and a walk-through show for the queue line. Each location has slight design differences, using a range of technology from century-old theatrical effects to modern special effects, including Audio-Animatronics. The attraction was in development for over a decade after the parks opened and was one of the last projects created under Walt Disney's direction. It inspired two distinct but loosely similar attractions: Phantom Manor at Disneyland Park Paris and Mystic Manor at Hong Kong Disneyland. Franchise media includes television specials, merchandise, comic strips, and two feature films: The Haunted Mansion released in 2003 and Haunted Mansion released in 2023. Guests enter through the front gate of a typical antebellum mansion, passing through gardens with a pet cemetery and a carriage led by an invisible horse. The deep voice of the Ghost Host introduces himself in the foyer. Guests enter an art gallery with four paintings showing people from the chest up; as the room stretches vertically, the portrait frames elongate, revealing the subjects' grim yet humorous fates. This room is actually an elevator transporting guests beneath the railroad berm to the main attraction. The room goes dark, the ceiling vanishes, and lightning flashes to reveal the cupola, where the Ghost Host's skeletal corpse hangs from the rafters by a noose, implying suicide; a shriek follows, then bones shatter. The Ghost Host apologizes, a wall opens, exposing a portrait corridor leading to the loading area—this corridor is a tunnel under the Disneyland Railroad to the ride building. The portraits on the right briefly flicker into macabre versions when lighting flashes from the left. At the corridor's end are two busts that appear to "follow" guests due to the Hollow-Face illusion. In the loading area, Doom Buggies descend one staircase and ascend another to the second floor, with fog pumped into the back. Guests pass a candelabra floating down an endless hallway, near which is a moving suit of armor and a chair with an abstract face. The Doom Buggies then view a glass conservatory with dead flora surrounding a casket; the occupant is heard calling for help, with bony hands trying to pry the lid open. The vehicles travel down a hallway of doors where sounds of pounding, calls for help, screams, knocking, and maniacal laughter are heard; knockers and handles move independently, and some doors appear to "breathe." A demonic grandfather clock chimes 13 as the minute hand spins backward, with a shadow of a claw passing over it. Guests enter a dark séance room with occult objects; Madame Leota, a blue-haired medium with a disembodied head in a levitating crystal ball, summons spirits, and floating musical instruments respond to her spell. After the séance, guests move to a mezzanine overlooking a massive ballroom where ghosts are enjoying a birthday party. Ghosts fly in from a crashed hearse and windows; one ghost girl blows out the candles, and the others disappear and reappear when she inhales. Drunken ghosts play with glasses of red wine on the chandelier; six ghost couples waltz to music from a gentleman's spirit on a pipe organ, with wraiths emerging from its pipes. Two duelists' portraits on the wall come to life and fire their revolvers. In the attic, guests see portraits of a bride with different grooms, each disappearing and reappearing; a shadow of a pianist plays a sinister version of the "Bridal March." The ghost of bride Constance Hatchaway floats nearby, holding the same candelabra as earlier, with her heart glowing pink and beating in time with the music. The Doom Buggies drift out of an attic window onto a balcony under a starry night sky, then fall backward beneath dead trees with humanoid faces. On reaching the ground, they turn toward a private graveyard where a frightened caretaker holds a lantern and shovel, with a scrawny dog cowering at his feet, whimpering. Around the corner, ghosts rise and party; comical scenes include a skeleton's hand popping from a tomb, a duo singing opera, a king and queen balancing on a gravestone, and a duchess sipping tea. Five busts sing the theme song "Grim Grinning Ghosts" near the end. The Doom Buggies enter a large crypt where the Ghost Host warns about hitchhiking ghosts as vehicles pass a group of three ghosts thumbing for a ride; in large mirrors, guests see one of the trio inside their buggy. Guests then disembark and begin leaving the mansion; a small ghost named Little Leota encourages them to return and to bring their "death certificate." The Haunted Mansion opened on day one at Magic Kingdom in Walt Disney World, located in Liberty Square. During production, duplicates of props and audio-animatronics were made for the Florida version, which was decided to be longer and more elaborate than the California version, with extra scenes like the library and music room. Paul Frees recorded additional voice-overs, including the Ghost Host, for these scenes. Due to more space in the park, the show building is larger and not restricted by a railroad berm. In the Foyer, there is a portrait of the Aging Man from the Disneyland version. Unlike the California version, the stretching rooms do not use elevators; instead, ceilings rise. After this, the door opens to the Doom Buggy loading area. Upon boarding, guests pass under a staircase with a floating candelabra, then pass changing portraits as seen in the Disneyland queue. An on-ride photo is taken here. Guests then enter the library, where ghost writers' busts stare and follow them. In the music room, an invisible pianist plays a sinister version of "Grim Grinning Ghosts," and guests proceed to the Endless Staircase, where footprints are visible and candelabras are occasionally blown out by unseen ghosts. Passing bat-eyed wallpaper that glows in the dark, guests see the Endless Hallway, with the Hatbox Ghost appearing next to it from a blue door, his footprints visible. After passing through the conservatory where a corpse cries for help, guests travel through a corridor of doors, where a demonic grandfather clock chimes 13. Guests enter the seance room, where Madame Leota floats and recites her spell, with instruments playing and a green specter floating alongside. The Doom Buggies enter the mezzanine of the ballroom, where ghosts gather for a party, then proceed to the attic. A piano player can be heard but not seen; the bride is now blue and white with a stained hatchet. The Doom Buggies pass through the cemetery, where ghosts sing "Grim Grinning Ghosts," and enter the crypt, where hitchhiking ghosts play in mirrors. Little Leota appears above the vehicles as guests disembark and pass a mausoleum and a pet cemetery. The Tokyo Disneyland version opened on day one and is located in Fantasyland; it is largely a duplicate of the Magic Kingdom version, with minor differences such as a haunted painting of a man resembling Peter Lorre whose face pops out and stretches, a tall, legless ghost in the Séance Room, and more advanced lighting. It did not receive the 2007 refurbishment changes made to the Magic Kingdom version. The idea for the Mansion predates Disneyland and WED Enterprises, originating when Walt Disney hired his first Imagineers. In 1951, a park illustration showed a main street, green fields, western village, and a carnival. Disney Legend Harper Goff developed a sketch of a crooked street leading to a peaceful church and graveyard, with a run-down manor perched high on a hill. Disney assigned Imagineer Ken Anderson to develop a story using Goff's idea. Plans were made for a New Orleans-themed land between Frontierland and Adventureland, promising a thieves' market, pirate wax museum, and a haunted house walk-through. Anderson studied New Orleans and old plantations, landing on the Shipley-Lydecker House in Baltimore, Maryland, and created a drawing of an antebellum manor with overgrown weeds, dead trees, swarms of bats, and a screeching cat as a weathervane. Disney rejected the idea of a run-down building. He visited the Winchester Mystery House in San Jose, California, and was captivated by its massive structure with stairs to nowhere, doors opening to walls and holes, and elevators. Anderson envisioned stories including a ghostly sea captain who killed his nosy bride and hanged himself, a family's misfortune, and a ghostly wedding party with Disney villains and spooks. In 1961, handbills announced a 1963 opening at Disneyland. Construction began a year later, with the exterior completed in 1963. The attraction was previewed in a 1965 episode of Walt Disney's Wonderful World of Color, but did not open until 1969, due to Disney's involvement in the 1964–1965 New York World's Fair and the attraction redesign after his death in 1966. After the fair, Imagineers Marc Davis, X Atencio, and Claude Coats contributed ideas; Anderson had left the project. Rolly Crump presented designs including coffin clocks, candle men, talking chairs, man-eating plants, tiki-like busts, living gypsy wagons, and a mirror with a face. Disney accepted these ideas and wanted to create a "Museum of the Weird," a restaurant side to the Haunted Mansion, similar to Blue Bayou at Pirates of the Caribbean. When Disney assigned Crump and Yale Gracey to create illusions, they intended to make the "Museum of the Weird" a separate walk-through section using the Pepper's ghost technique. Crump and Gracey were given a large workshop to develop their ideas. One night, they played a prank on the night cleaning crew by leaving lights on with motion sensors that triggered ghost effects; the next morning, the janitors found the effects still running and a broom in the center. Davis and Coats disagreed on whether the ride should be frightening or funny: Coats wanted a scary adventure with moody, bleak environments; Davis proposed a silly, gag-filled experience. Atencio combined both approaches, creating a transition from dark foreboding to spirited entertainment. The ride narration was performed by Paul Frees as the Ghost Host; the theme song "Grim Grinning Ghosts" was composed by Buddy Baker with lyrics by Atencio and is heard in nearly every area. After Disney's death in December 1966, the project evolved significantly. The "Museum of the Weird" idea was abandoned. Imagineers objected to a walk-through attraction's low capacity, suggesting two identical attractions to serve twice as many guests. A solution emerged with the development of the Omnimover system for Adventure Thru Inner Space, renamed the Doom Buggy. The system's continuous chain of semi-enclosed vehicles offered high capacity and allowed control over what guests saw and heard. Each car holds one to three people, making it ideal for the story of individuals wandering alone through a haunted house. Employee previews occurred on August 6, 7, and 8, followed by soft openings on August 9 and 10, and a "Midnight" Press Event on August 11. The attraction officially opened to all guests on August 12, 1969. Around 1977, WDI considered using Rolly Crump's unused designs and effects for Professor Marvel's Gallery, a tent show in Discovery Bay, but the expansion plans were dropped. In 1994, Disneyland's Haunted Mansion was updated with a phantom piano player in the attic and a full-fleshed bride replacing the original faceless one. In 2001, a new, more detailed safety spiel was added to the Doom Buggies' onboard audio, recorded by Joe Leahy in English and Fabio Rodriguez in Spanish, in a recreation of Paul Frees' Ghost Host voice, as part of a park-wide safety campaign. The seasonal overlay Haunted Mansion Holiday premiered in October, featuring characters from the 1993 film The Nightmare Before Christmas. In 2004, the Seance Room was updated so the crystal ball with Madame Leota's talking head floated above the table instead of sitting on it, with the original projection-mapped effect replaced by a rear-projection effect. In 2006, the original attic bride was replaced by Constance Hatchaway with a new storyline. In 2007, the attraction was renovated with the addition of changing portraits and lightning-filled windows from the Disneyland version, and new vocals for most of the graveyard ghosts. In the Walt Disney World version, an endless staircase was added after a dark space with spider webs. The Sinister 11 portraits, originally with eyes that stared at guests, were moved to the loading area during the refurbishment and no longer follow guests. In March 2011, a new "interactive queue" debuted at Walt Disney World, featuring crypts and tombstones honoring Imagineers; a murder mystery involving the sinister Dread Family; the Composer Crypt with musical instruments that play variations of "Grim Grinning Ghosts" when touched, including a pipe organ named after Thurl Ravenscroft; the Mariner's brine-filled sepulcher, whose ghost sings and sneezes; and a crypt for poetess Prudence Pock, featuring haunted moving books and Prudence's ghost writing invisibly in her poem book. Guests can solve unfinished poems by speaking into microphones. The FastPass+ line skips the queue and leads directly to the Foyer doors. There is also an extended queue using the former Mike Fink Keel Boats dock. On April 10, 2015, it was officially confirmed that The Hatbox Ghost would return to Disneyland's Haunted Mansion. The character returned on May 9, 2015. The Hatbox Ghost was originally part of the attraction when it opened in 1969 but was removed because the illusion was not convincing. The character was added to Disney World's Haunted Mansion on November 30.

The Haunted Mansion at Disneyland features the "Ravenscroft" company, named for Thurl Ravenscroft, one of the vocalists for "Grim Grinning Ghosts"; a brine-filled sepulcher where a ghost sings and sneezes; and a crypt dedicated to Prudence Pock, the poetess, which includes haunted moving books and Prudence's ghost writing invisibly in her poem book. Guests can solve unfinished poems by speaking into microphones located in the crypt. The FastPass+ line skips the queue entirely and leads guests directly to the Foyer doors. An extended queue line uses the former Mike Fink Keel Boats dock. On April 10, 2015, it was confirmed that The Hatbox Ghost would return to Disneyland's Haunted Mansion, debuting on May 9, 2015; the character was originally part of the attraction when it opened in 1969 but was removed due to an unconvincing illusion; it was added to Disney World's Haunted Mansion on November 30, 2023, as part of The Walt Disney Company's 100th Anniversary celebration. On April 2, 2019, PhotoPass ride photography was introduced at Magic Kingdom, with a hidden camera capturing riders as they pass the final portrait, the flash disguised as flickering lightning, and a black-and-white photo framed by surrounding ghosts automatically added to the guest's PhotoPass account via RFID from their second-generation MagicBand. On January 21, 2020, Disneyland's Haunted Mansion closed for an extensive refurbishment to install lighted steel panels, improved lighting, mechanical touch-ups, and new paint and trims, originally scheduled for completion in spring 2020 but delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic; it reopened on April 30, 2021, with a refreshed pet cemetery featuring new greenery, new drapes in the portrait gallery, more decorative wallpaper in the loading area, and the return of the original portrait "April to December," along with a statue of the one-eyed cat; the rest of the attraction received repairs and new lighting. A new secret entrance was added using an exit: once the crypt door opens, visitors go down a flight of stairs and through a utility passageway used by cast members. In January 2024, the Disneyland Haunted Mansion began another major refurbishment to expand the outdoor queue, modify nearby Magnolia Park in New Orleans Square, and add a gift shop at the ride's exit; the expansion opened on November 26, 2024, including an accessible elevator, and the gift shop, themed as the mansion's carriage house, opened on December 23, 2024. In January 2025, the attraction received a new bride inspired by the original character and storyline, and the hitchhiking ghosts scene was updated. The Haunted Mansion at Disneyland and Tokyo Disneyland transforms into Haunted Mansion Holiday during the Halloween and Christmas seasons since 2001, inspired by Tim Burton's 1993 film The Nightmare Before Christmas; it closes in mid to late August for a few weeks to revamp the attraction with new props and Audio-Animatronics from the movie, then reopens in September, closing again in early January to restore the original version and reopening late January. The Magic Kingdom does not have a holiday edition and operates continuously during the holidays. Disneyland Park Paris features Phantom Manor in Frontierland, a "re-imagined" version in Western Victorian, Second Empire style based on the Fourth Ward School House in Virginia City, Nevada, with a Western plot aligned with Thunder Mesa and Frontierland; unlike Disneyland and Magic Kingdom, which use English narration by Paul Frees, Phantom Manor features Vincent Price throughout. Mystic Manor opened at Hong Kong Disneyland in spring 2013 in Mystic Point, differing from the Haunted Mansion or Phantom Manor by not referencing departed spirits or the afterlife due to cultural differences in traditional Chinese culture; it continues the Society of Explorers and Adventurers theme of Tokyo DisneySea, telling the story of Lord Henry Mystic and his monkey Albert, who opens an enchanted music box that brings the house's artifacts to life; the exterior is a large Victorian mansion in Queen Anne style, with a trackless system and a musical score by Danny Elfman. On October 5, 2025, a woman in her 60s was found unresponsive after riding The Haunted Mansion; Disneyland security administered CPR until Anaheim Fire and Rescue arrived; she was transported to a local hospital and pronounced dead; no autopsy was performed, and no ride issues were found. Walt Disney Pictures produced two standalone live-action film adaptations: The first, The Haunted Mansion, directed by Rob Minkoff and starring Eddie Murphy, was released on November 26, 2003; the second, Haunted Mansion, directed by Justin Simien, was released on July 28, 2023. In July 2010, Guillermo del Toro announced he would write and produce a darker film adaptation, which was officially confirmed in July 2021, with Tiffany Haddish playing a hired psychic attempting to commune with the dead and LaKeith Stanfield playing a lackluster tour guide in New Orleans's French Quarter.
